etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English compellen, borrowed from Middle French compellir, from Latin compellere, itself from com- (“together”) + pellere (“to drive”). Displaced native Old English nīedan.

definitions.definition: (transitive, archaic, literally) To drive together, round up.

quote.citation: 1917, Upton Sinclair, chapter 16, in King Coal:
quote.text: She had one of those perfect faces, which irresistibly compel the soul of a man.

quote.citation: 1599 (first performance), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Iulius Cæsar”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: Against my will, / As Pompey was, am I compell’d to set / Upon one battle all our liberties.

quote.citation: 1827, Henry Hallam, The Constitutional History of England from the Accession of Henry VII. to the Death of George II. […], volume (please specify |volume=I or II), London: John Murray, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Wolsey  […]  compelled the people to pay up the whole subsidy at once.

quote.citation: 2020, N. K. Jemisin, The City We Became, Orbit, page 173:
quote.text: And then she giggles, inordinately pleased by her own cleverness.

quote.citation: December 15 2022, Samanth Subramanian, “Dismantling Sellafield: the epic task of shutting down a nuclear site”, in The Guardian‎[1]:
quote.text: Sellafield compels this kind of gaze into the abyss of deep time because it is a place where multiple time spans – some fleeting, some cosmic – drift in and out of view.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To exact, extort, (make) produce by force.

quote.citation: 1613 (date written), William Shakespeare, [John Fletcher], “The Famous History of the Life of King Henry the Eight”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii]:
quote.text: Commissions, which compel from each / The sixth part of his substance.

quote.citation: 1912, L. Frank Baum, chapter 14, in Sky Island:
quote.text: The Queen has nothing but the power to execute the laws, to adjust grievances and to compel order.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To force to yield; to overpower; to subjugate.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “(please specify the book number)”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Easy sleep their weary limbs compell'd.

quote.citation: 1859, Alfred Tennyson, “Enid”, in Idylls of the King, London: Edward Moxon & Co., […], →OCLC, page 79:
quote.text: And I will fetch you forage from all fields, / For I compel all creatures to my will.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To gather or unite in a crowd or company.

quote.citation: 1700, [John] Dryden, “Palamon and Arcite: Or, The Knight’s Tale. In Three Books.”, in Fables Ancient and Modern; […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book I, Canto I”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza 5:
quote.text: She had this knight from far compeld.

quote.citation: [1611?], Homer, “Book V”, in Geo[rge] Chapman, transl., The Iliads of Homer Prince of Poets. […], London:  […]  Nathaniell Butter, →OCLC; republished as The Iliads of Homer, Prince of Poets, […], new edition, volume I, London: Charles Knight and Co., […], 1843, →OCLC:
